text:
“My friend, your letter made us all weep. Let those noble hearts toward whom your good angel is guiding you know this: a mother and a poor young woman will pray to God for them morning and evening; and if the most fervent prayers rise to His throne, they will obtain some favors for all of you. Yes, my brother, their names are engraved upon my heart. Ah! I shall see them someday. I shall go, even if I have to make the journey on foot, to thank them for their friendship toward you, for it has poured balm, as it were, upon my raw wounds. Here, my friend, we are working like poor laborers. My husband, that great unknown man whom I love more with each passing day as, from moment to moment, I discover new riches in his heart, is neglecting his printing house, and I can guess why: your poverty, ours, and our mother’s are killing him. Our adored David is like Prometheus devoured by a vulture, a sallow grief with a sharp beak. As for him, the noble man, he scarcely thinks of it; he has hopes of a fortune. He spends all his days conducting experiments on the manufacture of paper; he has asked me to attend to the business in his stead, in which he helps me as much as his preoccupation allows. Alas! I am with child. This event, which would have filled me with joy, saddens me in the situation in which we all find ourselves. My poor mother has grown young again; she has recovered the strength needed for her exhausting work as a nurse. Were it not for our financial worries, we should be happy. Old Father Séchard will not give his son a farthing; David went to see him to borrow a little money from him so as to help you, for your letter had driven him to despair. ‘I know Lucien; he will lose his head and do foolish things,’ he said. I scolded him thoroughly. My brother, fail in any way whatsoever?... I replied to him, Lucien knows that I should die of grief. Without David’s suspecting it, my mother and I have pawned a few things; my mother will redeem them as soon as she comes into some money. In this way we have managed to raise one hundred francs, which I am sending you by the coach service. If I did not answer your first letter, do not be angry with me, my friend. We were in a situation that kept us up at night; I was working like a man. Ah! I did not know I had so much strength. Madame de Bargeton is a woman without soul or heart; even if she no longer loved you, she owed it to herself to protect and help you after tearing you from our arms only to cast you into that dreadful Parisian sea, where one needs a blessing from God to encounter true friendships amid those waves of men and interests. She is not to be regretted. I wanted some devoted woman beside you, a second self of mine; but now that I know you have friends who carry on our feelings, I am at peace. Spread your wings, my beloved, beautiful genius! You will be our glory, as you are already our love.

“EVE.”


“My darling child, after what your sister has told you, I can only bless you and assure you that, alas! my prayers and thoughts are filled with you alone, to the detriment of those whom I see; for there are hearts in which the absent are in the right, and so it is in the heart of

“YOUR MOTHER.”

Thus, two days later, Lucien was able to repay his friends the loan they had so graciously offered him. Perhaps life had never seemed more beautiful to him, but the stirring of his self-esteem did not escape his friends’ penetrating eyes and delicate sensibility.

“You would think you were afraid of owing us anything,” exclaimed Fulgence.

“Oh! the pleasure he displays is very serious in my eyes,” said Michel Chrestien; “it confirms the observations I have made: Lucien is vain.”

“He is a poet,” said d’Arthez.

“Do you hold it against me that I feel something as natural as this?”

“We must give him credit for not having concealed it from us,” said Léon Giraud. “He is still candid; but I am afraid that later he may come to fear us.”

“And why?” asked Lucien.

“We read your heart,” replied Joseph Bridau.

“There is in you,” Michel Chrestien told him, “a diabolical mind with which you will justify in your own eyes the things most contrary to our principles: instead of being a sophist of ideas, you will be a sophist of action.”

“Ah! I am afraid so,” said d’Arthez. “Lucien, within yourself you will conduct admirable debates in which you will be noble, and which will end in blameworthy deeds... You will never be in agreement with yourself.”

“And on what, then, do you base your indictment?” asked Lucien.

“Your vanity, my dear poet, is so great that you even put it into your friendship!” exclaimed Fulgence. “All vanity of that kind betrays a dreadful selfishness, and selfishness is the poison of friendship.”

“Oh! my God,” exclaimed Lucien, “you cannot know how much I love you.”

“If you loved us as we love one another, would you have shown such eagerness and made such a show of returning what it gave us so much pleasure to give you?”

“Here we do not lend anything to one another; we give,” Joseph Bridau told him bluntly.

“Do not think us harsh, my dear child,” Michel Chrestien told him; “we are being farsighted. We are afraid that one day we shall see you preferring the joys of some petty revenge to the joys of our pure friendship. Read Goethe’s Tasso, the greatest work of that splendid genius, and you will see in it that the poet loves brilliant fabrics, feasts, triumphs, splendor: well then, be Tasso without his madness. Will the world and its pleasures call to you? Stay here... Transfer to the realm of ideas everything your vanities demand. If there must be folly, put virtue into your actions and vice into your ideas, instead of thinking well and behaving badly, as d’Arthez was telling you.”

Lucien lowered his head: his friends were right.

“I confess that I am not as strong as you are,” he said, casting an adorable glance at them. “I do not have the back and shoulders to bear up under Paris, to struggle courageously. Nature has given us different temperaments and faculties, and you know better than anyone the reverse side of vices and virtues. I am already weary, I confess it to you.”

“We shall support you,” said d’Arthez. “That is precisely what faithful friendships are for.”

“The help I have just received is precarious, and we are all as poor as one another; need will soon pursue me again. Chrestien, in the pay of the first comer, can do nothing in the book trade. Bianchon stands outside that circle of business. D’Arthez knows only publishers of scientific or specialized works, who have no influence over publishers of new literature. Horace, Fulgence Ridal, and Bridau work in a realm of ideas that places them a hundred leagues away from publishers. I must decide on a course.”

“Then adhere to ours: suffer!” said Bianchon. “Suffer courageously and put your trust in Work!”

“But what is only suffering for you is death to me,” Lucien said sharply.

“Before the cock has crowed three times,” said Léon Giraud with a smile, “this man will have betrayed the cause of Work for that of Idleness and the vices of Paris.”

“Where has work brought you?” said Lucien, laughing.

“When one leaves Paris for Italy, one does not find Rome halfway there,” said Joseph Bridau. “For you, green peas ought to grow already dressed with butter.”

“They grow that way only for the eldest sons of peers of France,” said Michel Chrestien. “But we sow and water them ourselves, and find them better.”

The conversation became jocular and moved to another subject. Those discerning minds, those sensitive hearts sought to make Lucien forget this little quarrel, and from then on he understood how difficult it was to deceive them. He soon fell into an inward despair that he carefully concealed from his friends, believing them to be implacable mentors. His southern temperament, which ran so easily over the keyboard of feelings, led him to make the most contradictory resolutions.
